Which one?
Imagine standing in the middle
of an ocean of sand.
The sun is overhead,
the ground shimmers with heat,
and the horizon is empty in every direction.
Rain may not fall here for years.
Everything about this place says
that water is impossible.
And yet, somewhere out in this
emptiness, there are pools of clear
water ringed by green palm trees.
How can that be?
For desert travelers, a glimpse
of green on the horizon could be
a cruel trick.
A mirage happens when light bends
as it passes through layers of
hot air near the ground,
so the sky itself seems to shimmer
like a lake.
But sometimes the water is real.
It rises out of the dry ground,
day after day, year after year.
We call these places oases.
An oasis is an island of plants
and water in a sea of dry land.
Birds, insects and mammals gather here.
Date palms shade the springs,
and people have farmed around some
oases for thousands of years.
But this raises a simple question.
If it almost never rains in the
desert, where does all this water come from?
Let's follow it, step by step.
First, why are deserts so dry?
Many of the world's great deserts,
including the Sahara and the Arabian
Desert, sit near thirty degrees
north or south of the equator.
There, air that rose over the
tropics sinks back toward the ground.
Sinking air warms and dries out,
so clouds struggle to form.
Rain can fail for years,
the ground can bake far hotter
than the air above it,
and any water left on the surface
quickly evaporates.
If the sky is dry,
the answer is not in the sky.
The secret of most oases is underground.
A desert is not just a pile of sand.
Beneath the dunes lie layers of
rock laid down over millions of
years: sandstone, limestone, clay and shale.
Some of those layers can hold
enormous amounts of water,
and move it slowly over great distances.
Rocks like sandstone are full of
tiny spaces between their grains,
and limestone is often cracked
and hollowed out.
Water can soak into these spaces
and slowly move through them.
A layer of rock that holds and
passes water like this is called an aquifer.
Think of it as a sponge made of stone.
Some aquifers are vast.
The Nubian Sandstone Aquifer System
lies under parts of Egypt,
Libya, Sudan and Chad.
How does water get into an aquifer
in the first place?
Often, it starts far away.
Rain and melting snow fall on
mountains or higher ground at the
edge of a desert.
Some of that water seeps into cracks
and into rock layers that come
up to the surface there.
Then gravity takes over,
and the water begins a very slow
journey underground, sometimes
for hundreds of kilometers.
Along the way, it can take thousands
of years to reach the place where
it finally comes back to the surface.
Not every rock lets water through.
Clay and shale are so tight that
water barely moves through them.
Geologists call layers like these aquitards.
When a water-bearing layer is
sandwiched between two tight layers,
the water is trapped.
If the place where it entered is
higher than the land further along,
the trapped water is under pressure.
This is called a confined,
or artesian, aquifer.
Think of a garden hose with one
end held high.
Water pushes down from above,
and the lower end is under pressure.
In an artesian aquifer,
the weight of the water upslope
does the pushing.
If a crack or a fault breaks
through the rock above it,
water can rise to the surface on
its own, with no pump at all.
Many springs in desert oases are
fed this way.
One famous example is Siwa,
in Egypt's Western Desert,
near the Libyan border.
Siwa lies in a depression below
sea level, and by some counts it
has more than a thousand springs.
Its water comes from the Nubian
Sandstone Aquifer System.
Studies suggest the water feeding
Siwa's springs has spent tens of
thousands of years underground.
Around it grow date palms and olive
trees, and beside them lie salty lakes.
But where did so much underground
water come from, in a place this dry?
Part of the answer lies in the past.
Roughly eleven thousand to six
thousand years ago, the Sahara
was not a desert.
It was a green savanna with lakes and rivers.
Rock art in the Sahara shows
elephants, giraffes and hippos.
A stronger African monsoon reached
far north, bringing regular summer rain.
Earth's orbit slowly wobbles,
and that wobble changes how much
summer sunshine falls on North Africa.
As the sunshine weakened,
the monsoon retreated south,
and the Sahara dried out.
But water that had soaked into
the ground during this and earlier
wet periods stayed there.
Deep aquifers that receive almost
no new rain today still hold it.
This ancient water is called fossil water.
How old is this water?
Scientists can tell by measuring
rare radioactive atoms dissolved in it.
Water feeding the springs of Siwa
is thought to be around thirty
thousand to fifty thousand years old.
In 2004, a team used krypton-81
to date water from the Nubian
aquifer elsewhere in Egypt's Western
Desert, and found ages of two
hundred thousand to one million years.
It moves north only about one to
two meters a year.
Pressure is not the only way to
make an oasis.
Wind can do it too.
In open desert, strong winds blow
loose sand and dust away,
again and again, for thousands of years.
Where the rock is weak,
especially where salt crystals
break it apart, the ground can
be lowered bit by bit.
Geologists call this removal of
loose material by wind deflation.
Below every desert there is a level
called the water table.
Beneath it, the spaces in the rock
are full of water.
If wind lowers the ground far
enough, the bottom of the hollow
can reach that level.
Then water seeps out at the surface,
and marshes, salt flats or small lakes appear.
The wind has dug down to the water.
The most dramatic example is the
Qattara Depression in northwestern Egypt.
Its lowest point lies about one
hundred thirty-three meters below
sea level, one of the lowest places in Africa.
Scientists think wind, together
with salt weathering, removed the
rock that once filled it.
Its floor is covered by salt marshes
and salt flats, kept damp where
groundwater comes close to the surface.
Faults can also create oases.
A fault is a break in the
Earth's crust where rock has moved.
Along some faults, ground-up rock
and clay form a barrier,
like an underground dam.
Groundwater flowing toward the
fault is blocked and pushed upward.
Where it reaches the surface,
a line of springs can appear,
so oases sometimes sit in a neat
row along the fault.
You can see this in California's
Coachella Valley.
There, desert fan palms,
the only palm native to the western
United States, grow in groves right
along the San Andreas Fault.
Crushed rock in the fault zone
blocks groundwater and brings it
near the surface.
Thousand Palms Oasis is one of these groves.
One of the most famous earthquake
faults on Earth is also what keeps
these palms alive.
Even the driest deserts get rain
now and then, often as short, violent storms.
Hard, dry ground cannot soak it
up fast enough, so the water rushes
downhill as a flash flood.
These floods pour into dry valleys
called wadis.
They can be deadly.
But they also feed the ground
beneath the valley floor.
As a flood races down a wadi,
part of the water sinks into the
sand and gravel of the valley floor.
Long after the surface dries,
water can remain below,
shaded from the sun,
slowly moving downstream.
Where this hidden flow comes close
to the surface, wells can reach
it, and palms and gardens can grow.
Many oases sit in wadis for exactly
this reason.
Some deserts are crossed by rivers
that start somewhere much wetter.
The Nile is the great example.
Most of the water that reaches
Egypt comes from rain in the
Ethiopian Highlands, carried by
the Blue Nile.
As the river runs north through
the desert, it creates a narrow
green strip of farmland.
In a way, the Nile valley is
one very long oasis,
watered by rain that fell far away.
Once water appears, how do plants get there?
Some seeds are carried by wind.
Others arrive with animals,
especially birds, which can spread
seeds in their droppings.
Birds crossing the desert are drawn
to water and green plants,
and they stop to drink and rest.
Over time, a bare spring can become
a green island.
The most important plant of many
oases is the date palm, Phoenix dactylifera.
It has a deep,
spreading root system that can
reach groundwater, and it tolerates
salty soil better than most crops.
It also gives fruit that stores
well, along with leaves and wood for building.
For thousands of years,
date palms have been the backbone
of oasis farming across North Africa
and the Middle East.
Date palms also change the climate
beneath them.
Their crowns shade the ground,
which keeps it cooler and slows evaporation.
Oasis farmers used this to grow
food in layers.
Tall palms stand on top.
Beneath them grow fruit trees such
as figs, pomegranates and citrus.
And on the ground grow vegetables,
grains and fodder.
A single oasis garden can feed
far more people this way.
How big can an oasis get?
In eastern Saudi Arabia,
the Al-Ahsa Oasis holds about two
and a half million date palms.
UNESCO, which listed it as a World
Heritage Site in 2018,
describes it as the largest oasis
in the world.
For centuries it was watered by
natural springs and shallow wells,
and its canals, gardens and old
towns show how people organized
life around that water.
People also learned to make oases themselves.
In ancient Persia, engineers
developed the qanat, and settlements
depending on them existed by about
three thousand years ago.
Builders dug a well at the foot
of a hill to reach groundwater.
Then they dug a tunnel with a
gentle downhill slope from that
well to the fields below,
using a line of vertical shafts
for air and for hauling out soil.
Gravity did the rest.
Why underground?
Because in the desert,
open water evaporates quickly.
A canal on the surface would lose
much of its water to the sun and wind.
In a tunnel, the water stays cool
and much more of it arrives.
Qanats could carry water for many
kilometers, and some are still
in use today.
Iran's qanats are listed as a UNESCO
World Heritage Site.
The idea spread widely.
In the Sahara of Algeria,
these tunnels are called foggaras.
In Oman and the United Arab
Emirates, similar channels are called falaj.
In the Turpan Basin of western
China, they are known as karez.
And in Peru, the Nazca region has
its own underground channels, called puquios.
Across very different cultures,
people found the same solution
to the same problem.
Oases also shaped trade.
The Silk Road was not a single
road but a network of routes linked
by oasis towns.
Caravans carrying silk, spices
and other goods moved from one
water source to the next.
Cities such as Dunhuang in China,
Samarkand in Central Asia and
Palmyra in Syria grew rich as stops
along these routes.
Without their water, the
long-distance trade of the ancient
world would have looked very different.
Life in an oasis is a constant
struggle with the desert around it.
Crescent-shaped dunes called
barchans can creep forward with
the wind, burying fields,
houses and wells.
For centuries, oasis people have
fought back with fences of palm
fronds and rows of plants that
slow the sand.
Keeping an oasis alive takes work
every single year.
When the work stops,
sand can bury fields and choke
wells surprisingly fast.
There is a quieter danger, too.
All natural water carries some dissolved salt.
When irrigation water evaporates
under the desert sun,
the water leaves but the salt stays behind.
Year after year, salt builds up
in the soil until even hardy crops struggle.
This is called salinization.
That is why good drainage,
to carry salty water away,
matters as much in an oasis as
bringing water in.
In the twentieth century,
powerful pumps changed everything.
Deep wells could now lift fossil
water far faster than any natural spring.
In Saudi Arabia, from the 1980s,
center-pivot sprinklers turned
patches of desert into green circles
of wheat, some about a kilometer
across, watered by ancient groundwater.
Seen from space, the desert filled
with green dots.
But fossil water is like money
in a bank account that no longer
receives deposits.
Every liter pumped from a
non-renewable aquifer is a liter
that will not come back in our lifetimes.
In parts of North Africa and the
Arabian Peninsula, water levels
have dropped as pumping increased,
and some traditional springs and
qanats have weakened or dried up.
The most ambitious project of all
is Libya's Great Man-Made River,
begun in 1983.
It pumps fossil water from wells
deep in the Sahara and carries
it north to coastal cities through
buried concrete pipes four meters wide.
The planned network is nearly four
thousand kilometers long, designed
to deliver close to six million
cubic meters of water a day.
But that water comes from aquifers
that are barely being refilled.
Some desert countries now turn to the sea.
In Saudi Arabia, the United Arab
Emirates and elsewhere around the
Gulf, large plants remove salt
from seawater, increasingly using
a method called reverse osmosis,
which pushes water through very
fine membranes.
Desalination takes a lot of energy,
and it leaves behind very salty brine.
But for many coastal desert cities,
it has become a main source of drinking water.
In Chile's Atacama Desert,
one of the driest places on Earth,
rain almost never falls.
But along the coast,
thick fog drifts in from the Pacific.
Some communities hang large mesh
nets on hillsides.
Tiny fog droplets collect on the
mesh, merge into drops,
and trickle into gutters and pipes.
It is a small source of water,
but it comes straight out of the air.
Other projects work with the land itself.
Farmers and designers dig shallow
ditches along the contour of a
slope, called swales, to catch
the rare rain before it runs off.
They cover the soil with mulch
to keep it cool and moist,
and plant hardy trees.
In places like Jordan,
small demonstration sites have
shown that patches of dry land
can be made greener this way,
though it takes years of care.
Oases are also laboratories of evolution.
Just as remote islands produce
species found nowhere else,
so do isolated springs.
In Mexico's Chihuahuan Desert,
the Cuatro Ciénegas basin holds
hundreds of spring-fed pools.
More than one hundred fifty species
of plants and animals there are
found nowhere else, including fish,
snails and the only box turtle
that lives in water.
Some pools even contain
stromatolites, layered mats built by microbes.
For wildlife, an oasis can mean
the difference between life and death.
Gazelles, foxes and many other
animals depend on scattered sources
of water in the desert.
Huge numbers of migrating birds
cross the Sahara twice a year,
and oases offer them food,
shade and water along the way.
Lose those green dots on the map,
and the journey becomes far harder.
Some water is still being discovered.
In November 1981, the Space Shuttle
Columbia carried an imaging radar
over the eastern Sahara.
In very dry sand,
the radar could see down several
meters, and it revealed ancient
river valleys buried beneath the
sand, some ten to fifteen kilometers wide.
Scientists nicknamed them radar rivers.
Such buried valleys help show where
water once flowed, and where
groundwater may still be found.
Pumping too much water has another cost.
In some aquifers, especially those
with layers of clay,
the water helps hold the ground up.
When it is pumped out,
those layers can compact,
and the land surface slowly sinks.
This is called land subsidence.
Part of that compaction is
permanent: even if water returns,
the squeezed clay may never store
as much again.
Traditional oasis communities
understood scarcity well.
Water was usually shared by strict
rules, often by time.
In some North African oases,
each family's share was measured
by simple water clocks.
In thirteenth-century Tozeur, in
what is now Tunisia,
the scholar Ibn Chabbat is credited
with writing detailed rules for
sharing the oasis water.
In the desert, fairness was a matter
of survival.
Today, oases face new pressure.
Hotter summers mean more evaporation
from pools, soils and leaves.
Growing towns and farms pump more groundwater.
In some regions, the surrounding
land is becoming drier and more degraded.
Scientists watch oases closely,
because they show early how fragile
life in dry places can be when
water runs short.
So how is an oasis made?
Not by a single lucky accident.
It can be rain that fell on
distant mountains, or in a green
Sahara thousands of years ago.
It can be stored in sandstone and
held under pressure by clay.
It can rise through a fault,
appear where wind has dug down
to the water table,
or hide under the gravel of a wadi.
Many slow processes, working
together, bring water to the surface.
The next time you see a picture
of palm trees around a blue pool
in the desert, remember what lies beneath it.
Water that may have traveled for
centuries underground.
Water that may have fallen as rain
in a very different climate.
If you enjoyed this journey,
subscribing to Miya's Lab helps
us bring you the next hidden story
of our planet.
And tell us in the comments:
which oasis would you most like to visit?
